title: The death in the bath
hook: Tacitus tells of Seneca's slow death and Paulina's survival (Annals 15.63–64)

segments.voice: Yesterday: caelum, the letter to Helvia, and the sky over Corsica. Your line was the same sky. Did you look up, and think of someone far away? Day five hundred seventeen.

We've told the outline of this story before, back in year one: Nero's order, the friends at the table, the image of a life. Today we go back to Tacitus and read it more slowly, because the part people usually skip is the part about who was in the room. It's the year 65, at a country house four miles outside Rome. Seneca is at dinner with his wife, Paulina, and two friends, when the soldiers arrive. Today: the death in the bath.
screen: `WE'VE TOLD THE OUTLINE BEFORE.` → `WHO WAS IN THE ROOM?` → `THE DEATH IN THE BATH.`

segments.voice: First, Paulina. When the order comes, Tacitus says, Paulina declares that she will die with him. Seneca had spent years writing about not clinging to life, and he doesn't forbid her. He tells her he had shown her ways to go on living, but if she chooses this, he won't stand in the way of her courage. Second, the other room. Then Seneca does something quietly tender. He asks that she be taken to another room, so that neither of them, watching the other suffer, would lose heart. Even at the end, he's thinking about what being beside someone does to them. Third, the slow hours. Tacitus says Seneca's body was old and thin from plain living, and his life left it slowly. Through those hours he kept the people around him busy and steady. He called for his secretaries and dictated, and Tacitus doesn't repeat what he said, because it had already been published. At the last he was carried into a warm bath, and there he died. Fourth, Paulina lives. Nero, not wanting a reputation for extra cruelty, ordered her saved, and her household bound her wounds. Here Tacitus is careful. Some people at the time, he says, claimed she had sought death only while she believed Nero couldn't be softened. He reports the gossip, and then he tells us what he knows: she lived a few more years, faithful to her husband's memory, so pale it was plain how much life had drained from her. Tacitus doesn't make her a statue. He lets her be a person. And he leaves us a picture worth keeping: a death surrounded, start to finish, by people who stayed beside him.
screen: `PAULINA: I WILL DIE WITH YOU.` · `TAKE HER TO ANOTHER ROOM.` · `SLOW HOURS, STILL DICTATING.` · `PAULINA LIVES, PALE AND FAITHFUL.` · then, large: `BESIDE HIM.`

segments.voice: This is a heavy story, so go gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you'd want beside you on a hard day. Not the hardest day, just a hard one. Picture their face, their voice, the way they sit. Let yourself feel grateful that they exist. Then turn it around. Whose hard day could you sit beside? Hold that person for a few breaths too. The bell holds the time.
Paulina. Seneca's wife, who chose to die with him and was saved by Nero's order, living on faithful to his memory. Today's word.
Your line: beside him. Be beside someone today: a call, a visit, a message that says I'm here, to someone carrying something heavy. Day five hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Readers of Tacitus's account of Seneca's death often notice less the death itself than the people around him, and take from it a reminder to stay near those who are suffering.

fork.setup: you're Seneca. Paulina has chosen to stay with you to the end, and the hours are going slowly. what do you ask for?
options: that she stay in the room, holding your hand.
that she be taken to another room.
that the soldiers take her away by force.
fork.reveal: Tacitus says he asked that she be moved to another room, so neither would lose heart watching the other suffer.

trapdoor: what you thought: a noble Roman death scene.
what it means: a slow death full of people: a wife, friends, secretaries, all staying beside him.
what a scholar hears: Tacitus shapes Annals 15.60–64 with echoes of Socrates' death in Plato's Phaedo, yet keeps the gossip about Paulina in.

notes: Annals 15.60–64 paraphrased (Church & Brodribb 1876 is public domain but not on the validator list).
